explanations.explanation: Mercy it is, friend. David says he lifts his voice to the LORD "for mercy" (Psalm 142:1). He isn't coming with a list of demands or a speech about how deserving he is. He just asks, loud and plain, from the cave.

Good guess, since a lot of people pray for that one. But David's words in verse 1 are that he lifts his voice to the LORD "for mercy." Nothing in this psalm asks for years added. He's asking for the LORD's mercy right now, in that cave.

I get it, a crown is a big thing to ask for. But in this cave prayer, David doesn't mention a crown at all. He lifts his voice "for mercy" (Psalm 142:1). A hat was the last thing on my mind back when I was stuck in a drawer, too.

Nope, it's the opposite. David says, "I pour out my complaint before Him; I reveal my trouble to Him." (Psalm 142:2). He reveals his trouble to the LORD, so he isn't hiding it from Him. That's why this one is False.

False is right. David says, "I pour out my complaint before Him; I reveal my trouble to Him." (Psalm 142:2). He reveals his trouble to the LORD instead of hiding it. I think that's a pretty honest way to pray.

True! David says, "Although my spirit grows faint within me, You know my way." (Psalm 142:3). His spirit is fading, but he still knows one thing for sure. I think that's a good thing to hold onto when you're running low.

This one's true, friend. David says, "Although my spirit grows faint within me, You know my way." (Psalm 142:3). So even while he's fading, he tells the LORD that He knows his way. He doesn't say it the other way around.
A snare, yes. David says, "Along the path I travel they have hidden a snare for me." (Psalm 142:3). A snare is a trap. And he tells us it was hidden along his path.

Close in spirit, but that's not the word. David says "…they have hidden a snare for me." (Psalm 142:3). A spear and a snare are two different things. A snare is a trap, and David says it was hidden along his path.

Swords are scary, but David doesn't name one here. He says, "Along the path I travel they have hidden a snare for me." (Psalm 142:3). A snare is a hidden trap. Nobody hides a sword in the grass and hopes you trip over it.
That's it. David says, "Look to my right and see; no one attends to me." (Psalm 142:4). He tells the LORD to look, and what he says is that no one attends to him. I think that sounds lonely.

Not in this psalm, friend. David says, "Look to my right and see; no one attends to me." (Psalm 142:4). He doesn't name a friend there, only that no one attends to him. I think that's what makes the cave feel so empty.

His mighty men aren't named in this prayer. David says, "Look to my right and see; no one attends to me." (Psalm 142:4). So what he tells the LORD is that no one is attending to him. That's the whole point of what he's saying.

Other way around, friend. David says, "There is no refuge for me; no one cares for my soul." (Psalm 142:4). He doesn't see anyone around him who cares for his soul. That's a heavy line, and I think it hurts to read.

False is right. David says, "There is no refuge for me; no one cares for my soul." (Psalm 142:4). Nobody around him cares for his soul. That is a heavy thing to say out loud, and he says it straight to the LORD.

Refuge, baker! David cries to the LORD, "You are my refuge, my portion in the land of the living." (Psalm 142:5). A moment ago he said there was no refuge for him (Psalm 142:4). Now he says the LORD is his. A refuge is a safe place to run to.

I see why you'd go there, but that's not the word David uses. He says, "You are my refuge, my portion in the land of the living." (Psalm 142:5). He had just said there was no refuge for him (Psalm 142:4). So he turns to the LORD as the safe place he's looking for.

I see the thought, but that's not the word David uses. He says, "You are my refuge, my portion in the land of the living." (Psalm 142:5). Right after saying no one cares for his soul, he turns to the LORD and calls Him his refuge. A refuge is a safe place to run to.
Strong is right. David says, "Rescue me from my pursuers, for they are too strong for me." (Psalm 142:6). He doesn't pretend he can handle them. He says it plainly and asks the LORD to step in.

Not quite. The psalm says, "Rescue me from my pursuers, for they are too strong for me." (Psalm 142:6). David doesn't talk about their pride. He just says they're stronger than he is, and he asks the LORD to rescue him.

Clever would be a fun twist, but that's not what he says. David says, "Rescue me from my pursuers, for they are too strong for me." (Psalm 142:6). It's about strength. He admits he can't take them on, so he asks for rescue.
Prison, yes. David asks, "Free my soul from prison…" (Psalm 142:7). He's praying from a cave, and I think that word shows how shut in he feels. He wants out, and he asks the LORD to do the freeing.
The deep sea isn't in this psalm. David asks, "Free my soul from prison…" (Psalm 142:7). I think that word pictures being shut in. The ocean never comes up.

I can see the dry and lonely feeling, but that's not the word. David asks, "Free my soul from prison…" (Psalm 142:7). I think he's picturing being shut in, not wandering around outside. I bet he wants the LORD to open the door.
Praise! David asks, "Free my soul from prison, that I may praise Your name." (Psalm 142:7). He doesn't only want out for his own sake. He tells the LORD what he plans to do once he's free.
Not this time. David says, "Free my soul from prison, that I may praise Your name." (Psalm 142:7). He doesn't say anything about defending. What he wants to do with his freedom is praise.
Learning is a fine thing, baker, but it's not the word here. David says, "Free my soul from prison, that I may praise Your name." (Psalm 142:7). Praise is what he says he'll do once he's free.

The righteous, friend. David says, "The righteous will gather around me because of Your goodness to me." (Psalm 142:7). Remember, he said no one attended to him on his right (Psalm 142:4). Now he talks about a crowd gathering. That's a big turn from a lonely cave.

David does ask to be rescued from his pursuers (Psalm 142:6). But when he talks about who will gather, the word he uses is different. He says, "The righteous will gather around me because of Your goodness to me." (Psalm 142:7). The ones he names are the righteous.
Fancy guess, but kings aren't mentioned in this psalm. David says, "The righteous will gather around me because of Your goodness to me." (Psalm 142:7). The ones who gather are the righteous.

True! David says, "The righteous will gather around me because of Your goodness to me." (Psalm 142:7). He doesn't give the credit to himself. He points it to the LORD's goodness, and that's a fine way to end a cave prayer.

It's true, friend. David says, "The righteous will gather around me because of Your goodness to me." (Psalm 142:7). The reason he gives is the LORD's goodness to him. He doesn't say it's because of anything he did.
